Assign Cookies.problem: Each child needs one cookie of at least its greed value; each cookie serves at most one child. Maximize satisfied children.
Assign Cookies.approach: Sort both lists. Give the smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy remaining child. An exchange replacing a larger cookie with this one cannot hurt the child and preserves larger cookies for others.
Assign Cookies.complexity: O(n log n+m log m) time; O(n+m) copy space.
Assign Cookies.trace: Cookie 1 satisfies greed 1; second cookie 1 cannot satisfy greed 2.
Assign Cookies.pitfalls: Arrays are copied; zero children/cookies is valid. Values are assumed nonnegative.

Lemonade Change.problem: A drink costs 5. Customers pay 5,10,20 in order; start with no cash and return whether every change can be made.
Lemonade Change.approach: For a 20 bill prefer 10+5 over 5+5+5 because fives are the only way to change a future 10. Twenties never help make change.
Lemonade Change.trace: Three fives -> one ten consumes a five -> twenty uses ten+five.
Lemonade Change.pitfalls: Future bills cannot pay current change; do not aggregate the whole queue first.

Fractional Knapsack.problem: Items are [value,positive weight], nonnegative values. Fractions are allowed; maximize value within integer capacity.
Fractional Knapsack.approach: Sort by value per weight. An exchange of equal weight from a lower-density portion to a higher-density portion never decreases value, so consume densities in descending order.
Fractional Knapsack.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) copy space.
Fractional Knapsack.trace: Take 10 weight for 60, 20 for 100, then 20/30 of 120 for 80; total 240.
Fractional Knapsack.pitfalls: This greedy proof relies on divisible items. The 0/1 version requires a different algorithm.

Jump Game - I.problem: Nonnegative jump lengths allow any jump up to a[i]; determine whether last index is reachable from zero. Empty input is false.
Jump Game - I.approach: All indices up to far are reachable. If next i lies outside far there is a gap no prior jump crosses; otherwise update the frontier.
Jump Game - I.trace: At 0 frontier 2; at 1 frontier 4, reaching the last index.
Jump Game - I.pitfalls: Use long for i+a[i]. A singleton is reachable without a jump.

Shortest Job First.problem: All jobs arrive at time zero; nonpreemptive jobs have nonnegative durations. Return average waiting time.
Shortest Job First.approach: Run shortest duration first. Swapping a longer-then-shorter adjacent pair reduces the waiting contributed to the shorter job without changing later completion time.
Shortest Job First.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) copy space.
Shortest Job First.pitfalls: Different arrival times require scheduling with a priority queue; this contract has simultaneous arrivals.

Job sequencing Problem.problem: Each job takes one time unit and is [deadline,profit]. Maximize profit by completing before deadlines; return [jobs done,total profit]. Nonpositive-profit jobs may be skipped.
Job sequencing Problem.approach: Consider profit descending and schedule at the latest free slot before its deadline. This keeps earlier slots available for tighter deadlines. Unit-duration deadline scheduling admits this greedy exchange.
Job sequencing Problem.complexity: O(n log n+n*min(n,maxDeadline)) time; O(min(n,maxDeadline)) slot space plus sorted copy.
Job sequencing Problem.trace: Schedule profit 100 at slot 2, profit 27 at slot 1, profit 15 at slot 3; total 142.
Job sequencing Problem.pitfalls: The algorithm does not apply to variable-duration jobs. Deadlines <=0 are unschedulable.
Job sequencing Problem.alternatives: A disjoint-set latest-free-slot structure improves scheduling to near-linear after sorting.

N meetings in one room.problem: Maximize nonoverlapping meetings [start,end]. This variant requires the next start STRICTLY after the previous end.
N meetings in one room.approach: Always choose the earliest finishing compatible meeting. Replacing an optimal first choice with this earlier finisher leaves at least as much time for remaining meetings.
N meetings in one room.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) copy space.
N meetings in one room.pitfalls: Some judges allow touching endpoints; change > to >= for that contract. Equal finish times are harmless to count.

Non-overlapping Intervals.problem: Return minimum intervals to remove so remaining intervals do not overlap; touching endpoints are allowed.
Non-overlapping Intervals.approach: Maximize kept intervals with earliest finishing compatible choices, then subtract from total. The earliest-finish exchange argument proves the kept count is optimal.
Non-overlapping Intervals.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) copy space.
Non-overlapping Intervals.pitfalls: This contract uses >= unlike strict meeting scheduling.

Insert Interval.problem: Insert a closed interval and merge overlaps. This implementation accepts unsorted input too.
Insert Interval.approach: Append the new interval and reuse general sort-and-merge. Correctness follows from the merge invariant.
Insert Interval.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space.
Insert Interval.pitfalls: When original input is already sorted and disjoint, a three-phase scan gives O(n) time: copy before, merge overlaps, copy after.

Merge Intervals.problem: Merge overlapping closed intervals; touching endpoints merge. Return a new array.
Merge Intervals.approach: Sort by start. A new interval either extends the last merged block or starts a new disjoint block. Future starts cannot overlap earlier blocks without also reaching the last.
Merge Intervals.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) space.
Merge Intervals.trace: [1,3] and [2,6] combine to [1,6]; subsequent starts 8 and 15 create new blocks.
Merge Intervals.pitfalls: Use max on end: a contained interval must not shrink a block. Inputs are copied.

Minimum number of platforms required for.problem: Each train has arrival<=departure on the same day. Count minimum simultaneous platforms; an arrival exactly at a departure needs another platform.
Minimum number of platforms required for.approach: Sort event times independently and sweep. An arrival increases active platforms; a departure frees one. Maximum concurrent active trains is both necessary and sufficient.
Minimum number of platforms required for.complexity: O(n log n) time; O(n) copies.
Minimum number of platforms required for.trace: At 1100 the trains arriving 940,950,1100 overlap until 1120, requiring three.
Minimum number of platforms required for.pitfalls: Overnight trains need a normalized day-aware timeline. Change <= to < if touching times may reuse a platform.

Valid Paranthesis Checker.problem: For (,),* where * may be (,),or empty, decide if some replacement gives balanced parentheses.
Valid Paranthesis Checker.approach: Track a RANGE of possible open counts. * expands low down/high up; clamp low to zero because negative opens are invalid. If high becomes negative, every interpretation fails. At the end zero must be in the range.
Valid Paranthesis Checker.pitfalls: This is the wildcard-parentheses variant; ordinary bracket matching uses a stack.
Valid Paranthesis Checker.alternatives: Trying all three meanings of every star is O(3^stars). DP memoizes index/open states.

Candy.problem: Every child receives at least one candy; higher rating than either neighbor needs strictly more candy. Minimize total.
Candy.approach: Left-to-right enforces the left-neighbor constraint minimally. Right-to-left enforces the right constraint using max to preserve the left one. Each assigned count is the minimum satisfying both slopes.
Candy.pitfalls: Equal ratings impose no ordering requirement. Total needs long for long slopes.
Candy.alternatives: A slope-based one-pass method uses O(1) space but must carefully subtract the shared peak when joining ascent and descent.

Jump Game II.problem: Return the minimum jumps to the last index or -1 if unreachable, with nonnegative max jump lengths.
Jump Game II.approach: Process reachable indices in BFS-like layers. end is the boundary reachable with current jumps; far is the next layer frontier. Cross each layer boundary once.
Jump Game II.trace: First layer from index 0 reaches 2; scanning indices 1,2 extends next frontier to 4, requiring two jumps.
Jump Game II.pitfalls: Do not increment jumps for each frontier increase. Zero-length progress at a layer boundary means unreachable.

Greedy Minimum Coins for a Canonical Sys.problem: Minimum coins for the explicitly fixed canonical denominations1,2,5,10,20,50,100. Return coins descending.
Greedy Minimum Coins for a Canonical Sys.approach: Take the largest fitting denomination. For this decimal1/2/5 hierarchy, enough lower coins to replace a larger one can always be exchanged without using more coins; normalize these exchanges until the greedy counts remain.
Greedy Minimum Coins for a Canonical Sys.complexity: O(number of returned coins+7) time/output; O(1) auxiliary state.
Greedy Minimum Coins for a Canonical Sys.pitfalls: Greedy is not valid for arbitrary denominations:1,3,4 target6 greedily uses4+1+1, while3+3 is optimal. Use the DP Minimum coins lesson for general systems. This is an algorithmic coin system, not a claim about current currency circulation.
